messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame, a 37-year-old psychologist, found himself trapped in a life that felt increasingly suffocating. The traumatic event that forever altered his perception of safety occurred two years ago when he was attacked in a dimly lit parking garage after a late session. The experience haunted him both in waking life and in his dreams, replaying with a vividness that left him breathless. Since that night, Kwame felt as though he had been stripped of his autonomy, and he began to view the world through a lens of hopelessness. This pervasive sense of vulnerability led Kwame to interpret every experience as a potential threat, reinforcing his belief that he was always on the brink of danger. Having decided that he was permanently vulnerable, he walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with him before anything had happened. He was convinced that he would never truly feel safe again, and this belief seeped into every corner of his existence, shaping his reality in ways he could hardly articulate.

Kwame's days were punctuated by moments that served as painful reminders of his trauma. He dreaded being in confined spaces, such as the small office where he often met clients. The pervasive sense of threat he carried with him made even ordinary situations feel charged with potential danger, turning the familiar into a minefield of anxiety that set his heart racing. His heightened sense of threat made even ordinary situations feel charged with danger, transforming the mundane into a source of anxiety that he could not escape. The sensation of being locked in made his heart race, and he would find himself scanning the room, hyper-aware of the exits. Comments on sexual violence, whether in the media or casual conversations, would send shivers down his spine, triggering a cascade of memories that made him feel powerless. He avoided situations where he might find himself alone with men, as the mere thought of it filled him with an acute sense of vulnerability. This heightened sense of threat meant that even benign encounters were fraught with worry, causing him to perceive danger in moments that others would view as harmless. The conviction that he was exposed to others, that they could somehow perceive the darkness he carried within, only deepened his isolation. He often felt as if he wore a visible scar, one that marked him as a victim, forever altering how he interacted with those around him.

The threat of danger loomed large in Kwame’s mind. He could not relax, even in the comfort of his own home. Sleep eluded him, as he lay wide awake, the weight of alertness pressing down on him like a physical burden. He had come to believe that unless his back was against a wall, he was vulnerable to attack, a constant reminder of the helplessness he felt. This hyper-vigilance fed into his negative appraisals, reinforcing the narrative that he had no future worth looking forward to. The constant sense of danger became the most convincing evidence for Kwame that his life had changed irreparably, leading him to believe that he would always be vulnerable and never truly safe. Feeling this afraid all the time, he had eventually come to accept the conclusion his body kept offering: that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe. The world seemed fraught with peril, and he felt that no matter how hard he tried, he could not stop bad things from happening to him. This constant awareness of danger confirmed his deepest fears, solidifying his negative appraisals that he was destined to live in a world where safety was an illusion. It was as if the universe conspired against him, and he was left helpless in the face of that reality.

Kwame's professional life began to suffer as well. He found it increasingly difficult to maintain the empathy required to be an effective psychologist. His clients spoke of their struggles, but he could barely focus; all he could think about was his own turmoil. He began to withdraw from social engagements, fearing that others might inadvertently draw attention to his trauma. His friends, once a source of comfort, now felt like reminders of his inadequacies, reinforcing his belief that he was exposed and vulnerable. This sense of detachment from others only exacerbated his feelings of hopelessness, trapping him in a spiral where every negative thought fed into another.

As the months turned into years, Kwame found himself at a crossroads. The realization that he could no longer bear the weight of his trauma alone brought him to this moment of seeking help. In the solitude of his office, he sat with his thoughts, wrestling with the fear that seeking therapy might expose him further, that he would have to confront the very memories he fought so hard to suppress. Yet, there was a flicker of hope buried beneath the despair, a yearning to reclaim the life he once led. Kwame hoped that through therapy, he might find a way to navigate the darkness, to build a future where he could feel secure in his own skin again. What frightened him most was the thought that he might always feel this way, trapped in a cycle of fear and helplessness, unable to escape the shadows of his past.

violation_explanations: The relationship where negative appraisals lead to a sense of threat is not clearly established, as there is no indication that Kwame's negative beliefs directly influence his perception of danger.
The relationship where a sense of threat leads to negative appraisals is also absent, as the vignette does not show how Kwame's perceived threats contribute to his negative beliefs.
